main.title: Crazy Taxi 2
main.summary: Jumping taxis and group fares add new routes through two crowded cities, with every successful delivery buying another chance to keep driving.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Crazy Taxi 2 is Hitmaker's 2001 Dreamcast driving game and the sequel to Sega's arcade taxi racer. Four new cabbies take fares around the New York-inspired Around Apple and Small Apple maps. The Crazy Hop adds a jump to the familiar combination of racing against the clock, collecting passengers and finding a fast route to their destination.

cards.heading: A fare buys more time
cards.text: A waiting passenger starts another short deadline inside the larger run. Reach the destination quickly and the reward includes more time to keep working; arrive slowly and that opportunity shrinks. The next fare therefore matters before the current one has ended. Stopping near another customer can keep the run flowing, while a long detour may leave too little time to recover. The city becomes a chain of possible journeys, with each successful stop setting up the next decision.

cards.heading: Jump over the queue
cards.text: Crazy Hop lets the taxi leave the road with a button press. A line of traffic can become something to clear rather than a queue to drive around, and an elevated route becomes another possibility to judge at speed. The jump can also be combined with the driving manoeuvres. Group fares add several passengers to the same cab, increasing what can be earned while asking the driver to handle their successive destinations. Good handling and a useful route have to work together.

cards.heading: Practise the difficult manoeuvre
cards.text: Crazy Pyramid separates particular driving tasks from the bustle of collecting fares. Its short challenges give a manoeuvre or a timing problem a clear target, then open further tests as the lower rows are completed. Failure can be followed by another attempt at the same small problem. Returning to the city puts that practice into a less predictable setting, where the useful trick has to be chosen among traffic, corners and waiting passengers. The training and the main run reinforce each other.

main.title: Sonic Adventure 2
main.subtitle: Two sides of the same race
main.summary: Sonic and Shadow lead parallel campaigns that alternate fast platforming, mechanical shooting and treasure hunting.

cards.heading: Hero and Dark
cards.text: Sonic Adventure 2 is Sonic Team USA’s three-dimensional platform adventure, first released for Dreamcast in North America on 19 June 2001. Its Hero and Dark campaigns follow the same crisis from opposing sides. Sonic, Tails and Knuckles face Shadow, Doctor Eggman and Rouge, with the story eventually bringing their journeys together. Each side has a runner, a machine pilot and a treasure hunter. Moving between those roles changes the task as well as the character, making the campaign a succession of distinct kinds of stage.

cards.heading: Three ways through a stage
cards.text: Sonic and Shadow race through platforming courses, using homing attacks and grinding along rails. Tails and Eggman pilot armed machines, locking onto targets as they work through more deliberate shooting stages. Knuckles and Rouge search larger spaces for hidden objects, using radar and clues to narrow the search. The campaigns repeatedly return to these three patterns, so players learn related abilities on both sides of the story. Outside the missions, animals and items collected along the way can be taken into the Chao gardens.

cards.heading: A city with its own rhythm
cards.text: Sonic Team USA developed the game around its American surroundings, with San Francisco among the influences on the urban stages. City Escape opens with Sonic descending city streets before the route turns into a pursuit. The music gives the cast equally distinct identities, ranging from rock to rap and orchestral passages. Jun Senoue, Fumie Kumatani, Tomoya Ohtani and Kenichi Tokoi contributed to the score. Released around Sonic’s tenth anniversary, the game became his final new adventure made for a Sega console before its later adaptations.

main.title: Shadow Hearts
main.subtitle: An uneasy journey through 1913
main.summary: Shadow Hearts is Sacnoth's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 28 June 2001. Yuri Hyuga can transform into monsters, a power that draws him into the struggle surrounding Alice Elliot and a dangerous magician. Their journey crosses a fictional version of the early twentieth century where recognisable places coexist with supernatural threats. The party explores towns and hostile locations, then fights in turn-based encounters. Its combination of historical surroundings, disturbing creatures and eccentric companions gives the adventure a markedly different atmosphere from a conventional fantasy quest.

cards.heading: An uneasy journey through 1913
cards.text: Shadow Hearts is Sacnoth's PlayStation 2 role-playing game, first released in Japan on 28 June 2001. Yuri Hyuga can transform into monsters, a power that draws him into the struggle surrounding Alice Elliot and a dangerous magician. Their journey crosses a fictional version of the early twentieth century where recognisable places coexist with supernatural threats. The party explores towns and hostile locations, then fights in turn-based encounters. Its combination of historical surroundings, disturbing creatures and eccentric companions gives the adventure a markedly different atmosphere from a conventional fantasy quest.

cards.heading: Make the ring land
cards.text: Choosing an attack is only the beginning of a turn. A rotating indicator crosses marked sections of the Judgement Ring, and the player presses a button as it reaches the appropriate areas. Accurate timing determines whether the selected action succeeds and how well it works. The same idea extends beyond basic weapon attacks, keeping attention on the screen while the party takes its turns. Character abilities and equipment still require planning, but the ring makes execution something the player must perform rather than simply confirm.

cards.heading: The cost of a transformation
cards.text: Yuri's Fusion ability allows him to take on different monstrous forms, giving the party another set of powers to manage. The setting continues the world of Sacnoth's earlier Koudelka, with recurring connections beneath the new journey. Director and writer Matsuzo Machida drew on horror fiction and manga, while Yoshitaka Hirota's score mixed musical styles to support the unsettling tone. Reviewers responded to the story and timing system more warmly than to every part of the presentation. Shadow Hearts: Covenant continued Yuri's story in 2004.

main.title: Klonoa: Empire of Dreams
main.subtitle: A dreamer enters a land without dreams
main.summary: Klonoa: Empire of Dreams is Now Production's Game Boy Advance puzzle platformer placing the long-eared traveller in the Empire of Jillius, where dreaming has been forbidden. His journey uses compact two-dimensional stages built around catching and throwing enemies with the Wind Ring. The portable adventure gives the familiar character a more enclosed kind of challenge, with each room asking how its creatures and movable objects can help reach the necessary stars. Progress comes from understanding what can be carried and where that temporary resource needs to be used.

cards.heading: A dreamer enters a land without dreams
cards.text: Klonoa: Empire of Dreams is Now Production's Game Boy Advance puzzle platformer placing the long-eared traveller in the Empire of Jillius, where dreaming has been forbidden. His journey uses compact two-dimensional stages built around catching and throwing enemies with the Wind Ring. The portable adventure gives the familiar character a more enclosed kind of challenge, with each room asking how its creatures and movable objects can help reach the necessary stars. Progress comes from understanding what can be carried and where that temporary resource needs to be used.

cards.heading: An enemy is also another jump
cards.text: The Wind Ring draws a nearby enemy into Klonoa's grasp. From there, he can throw it toward another target or use it to perform a double jump, exchanging the carried creature for additional height. Large blocks can also be picked up and positioned to change a route. The same object can therefore have several possible purposes, and choosing one may remove another option. A successful sequence depends on keeping the useful resource available until the point where its throw, weight or contribution to a jump is actually required.

cards.heading: Three stars make the exit available
cards.text: Each stage requires three stars before its exit can be used, giving the small spaces a clear structure beyond simply moving toward the right edge of the screen. Optional crystals and hidden rewards invite a closer reading of the same arrangement. Klonoa can also briefly hover by flapping his ears, providing a little more control after leaving the ground. The combination allows a short stage to contain a careful sequence of decisions, where an apparently unreachable star becomes accessible once the correct enemy or block has been brought into position.

main.title: Final Fantasy X
main.summary: Final Fantasy X is a 2001 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Voices, CTB and the Sphere Grid
cards.text: Final Fantasy X is a 2001 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for PlayStation 2. The tenth main installment in the Final Fantasy series, it is the first game in the series to feature fully three-dimensional areas (though some areas were still pre-rendered), and voice acting. Final Fantasy X replaces the Active Time Battle (ATB) system with the "Conditional Turn-Based Battle" (CTB) system, and uses a new leveling system called the "Sphere Grid".

cards.heading: Tidus and Yuna confront Sin
cards.text: The game is set in the fantasy world of Spira, a setting influenced by the South Pacific, Thailand and Japan, while the name of the city of Samarkand in Uzbekistan has been cited as an inspiration for Zanarkand. The game's story revolves around a group of adventurers and their quest to defeat a rampaging monster known as Sin. The player character is Tidus, a star athlete in the fictional sport of blitzball, who finds himself in Spira after Sin destroyed his home city of Zanarkand. After meeting the summoner Yuna, Tidus embarks on a quest to destroy Sin, having discovered its true identity is that of his missing father, Jecht.

cards.heading: Three composers and a direct sequel
cards.text: Development began in 1999 with more than a hundred people and a budget exceeding $32 million. The music also expanded the team: Masashi Hamauzu and Junya Nakano composed alongside Nobuo Uematsu, the first main-series score not written entirely by him. Final Fantasy X shipped more than 8.5 million copies on PlayStation 2. Its 2003 follow-up, Final Fantasy X-2, made it the first entry to receive a direct game sequel. Later HD editions brought both adventures to further consoles and computers.

main.title: Mario Kart: Super Circuit
main.summary: Mario Kart: Super Circuit is a 2001 kart racing game for the Game Boy Advance (GBA).

cards.heading: Mario Kart: Super Circuit
cards.text: Mario Kart: Super Circuit is a 2001 kart racing game for the Game Boy Advance (GBA). It is the third Mario Kart game and retains its predecessors' gameplay: as a Mario franchise character, the player races opponents around tracks based on locales from the Super Mario platform games. Tracks contain obstacles and power-ups that respectively hamper and aid the player's progress. Super Circuit includes various single-player and multiplayer game modes, including a Grand Prix racing mode and a last man standing battle mode.

cards.heading: Intelligent Systems takes Mario Kart handheld
cards.text: Super Circuit was developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo. It was the first handheld Mario Kart game and the only game in the series developed by Intelligent Systems. Its graphical style changed drastically from early demos, with the final release resembling Super Mario Kart (1992) visually. Nintendo revealed Super Circuit alongside the GBA in 2000 and released it in mid-2001, months after the console's launch.

cards.heading: A GBA hit finds new platforms
cards.text: Super Circuit received acclaim, with praise for its modes, presentation, gameplay, and difficulty, though responses to the multiplayer were mixed. Retrospectively, critics have ranked it as one of the best GBA games, but one of the lesser Mario Kart games due to its lack of technical innovation compared to its predecessors. It was nominated for several awards and won one. Super Circuit sold 5.91 million copies worldwide, making it the fourth-bestselling GBA game. It was rereleased digitally for the Virtual Console line on the Nintendo 3DS in 2011 and the Wii U in 2014, and for the Nintendo Classics service in 2023.

main.title: Max Payne
main.summary: Max Payne is a 2001 third-person shooter game developed by Remedy Entertainment.

cards.heading: Max Payne
cards.text: Max Payne is a 2001 third-person shooter game developed by Remedy Entertainment. It was originally released for Windows by Gathering of Developers in July 2001. The game centers on former New York City Police Department (NYPD) detective Max Payne, who attempts to solve the murder of his family while investigating a mysterious new designer drug called "Valkyr". While doing so, Max becomes entangled in a large and complex conspiracy involving a major pharmaceutical company, organized crime, a secret society, and the United States Armed Forces. The game features a gritty neo-noir style and uses graphic novel panels with voice-overs as its primary means of storytelling, drawing inspiration from hard-boiled detective novels by authors like Mickey Spillane. It contains many allusions to Norse mythology, particularly the myth of Ragnarök and several names. The gameplay is heavily influenced by the Hong Kong action cinema genre, particularly the work of director John Woo, and it was one of the first games to feature the bullet time effect popularized by The Matrix (1999).

cards.heading: Max Payne moves across platforms
cards.text: Max Payne moved from Windows to PlayStation 2 and Xbox in December 2001, followed by a Mac edition in 2002. The 2003 Game Boy Advance adaptation changed the viewpoint to an isometric one while retaining much of the original action. A mobile version arrived in 2012 alongside Max Payne 3. Later digital releases and backward compatibility kept the earlier console versions playable on newer PlayStation and Xbox systems, allowing the original story to reach audiences beyond its first hardware.

cards.heading: Noir gunplay launches a franchise
cards.text: Max Payne received positive reviews from critics, and is often considered one of the greatest games ever made. Praise was directed at the game's exciting gunplay and use of noir storytelling devices, while some criticized its linear level design and short length. The game sold 4 million units. It won a large number of accolades, including a BAFTA Award for Best PC Game of 2001. Its success launched the Max Payne franchise, including the sequels Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne, developed again by Remedy and published by Rockstar in October 2003, and Max Payne 3, developed solely by Rockstar and released in May 2012. A loose film adaptation of the first game was released in October 2008. In 2022, it was announced that Remedy is developing remakes of Max Payne and Max Payne 2 for PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S, with Rockstar publishing.

main.title: Golden Sun
main.subtitle: A journey shaped by elemental power
main.summary: Golden Sun is Camelot's Game Boy Advance role-playing adventure following Isaac and his companions through the world of Weyard. Their elemental abilities, called Psynergy, are used both against enemies and to solve problems in the surrounding landscape. Towns, caves and ruins connect the journey's conversations with turn-based battles and environmental puzzles. The shared role of magic gives the adventure a clear identity: an ability learned for the party can also become the means of reaching another place, making character development useful beyond the next confrontation on the road.

cards.heading: A journey shaped by elemental power
cards.text: Golden Sun is Camelot's Game Boy Advance role-playing adventure following Isaac and his companions through the world of Weyard. Their elemental abilities, called Psynergy, are used both against enemies and to solve problems in the surrounding landscape. Towns, caves and ruins connect the journey's conversations with turn-based battles and environmental puzzles. The shared role of magic gives the adventure a clear identity: an ability learned for the party can also become the means of reaching another place, making character development useful beyond the next confrontation on the road.

cards.heading: A spell can change the route
cards.text: Psynergy allows characters to interact with objects and obstacles while exploring. A whirlwind can remove vegetation, while other abilities help move or transform something in the environment. Dungeons combine those powers with more conventional spatial tasks, such as pushing logs to make a crossing or changing the route of a mine cart. The player has to recognise which part of a scene is capable of responding. An elemental ability therefore becomes another way of reading the world, revealing practical connections between the party's powers and the objects placed along its route.

cards.heading: Small spirits change the party
cards.text: Elemental Djinn can be found and assigned to characters, changing their available abilities and development. Their use in battle also connects preparation with powerful summons, making the arrangement of the collection an important choice rather than a passive list of discoveries. The party's capabilities can shift as those spirits are redistributed. Golden Sun gives its journeys several linked forms of progress: another destination can reveal a new Djinni, that companion can change a character's options, and those options can help the group approach another battle or puzzle in a different way.

main.title: Tekken 4
main.summary: Tekken 4 is a 2001 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: Tekken 4
cards.text: Tekken 4 is a 2001 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades. Initially released for Namco's System 246 hardware, it was then ported to the PlayStation 2 home console in 2002. As the fourth main installment in the Tekken series following Tekken 3 (1997), and the fifth overall following the non-canon title Tekken Tag Tournament (1999), the game harbored many gameplay revisions, such as the series-unique ability for the player to move about before the round begins and the introduction of walled stages.

cards.heading: Kazuya returns to the tournament
cards.text: There are up to twenty-two playable characters, five of which are newcomers and one alter-ego palette swap. Placing distinction on the plot in the console version, the tone of Tekken 4 was noticeably darker than other installments in the series. The game notably features the canonical return of Kazuya Mishima, whose story reveals that he was revived following his death 20 years prior and has entered the King of Iron Fist Tournament 4 to take back the Mishima Zaibatsu from his father Heihachi Mishima and seek out his son Jin Kazama.

cards.heading: Uneven arenas divide the Tekken audience
cards.text: Tekken 4 received generally favorable reviews. Veteran arcade players and casual console players differed in their initial responses. Uneven floors, walls and an emphasis on lateral movement changed the space for aerial combos and juggling, dividing the competitive audience. There is also more aggression and poking, akin to boxing or fencing. However, there has been a revival in its reception becoming more positive for its innovative art design and sound. Meanwhile, critics and publications including IGN have rated it as one of the best games in the series. A sequel, Tekken 5, was released in 2004.

main.title: Wario Land 4
main.subtitle: Into the golden pyramid
main.summary: Wario Land 4 is Nintendo's 2001 Game Boy Advance platform game about a treasure hunt inside a golden pyramid. Its chambers lead to very different worlds, with gems, a key-carrying creature and a route home to find. Wario's strange reactions to enemies make his body part of each stage's machinery.

cards.heading: Into the golden pyramid
cards.text: Wario Land 4 is Nintendo's 2001 Game Boy Advance platform game about a treasure hunt inside a golden pyramid. Its chambers lead to very different worlds, with gems, a key-carrying creature and a route home to find. Wario's strange reactions to enemies make his body part of each stage's machinery.

cards.heading: Finding the way back
cards.text: Entering a stage closes the portal behind Wario. He searches for gem pieces that unlock the boss door and finds the Keyzer needed for the next stage. There is room to explore before pressing the frog switch, which reopens the exit and starts a countdown. The route just travelled becomes a return journey under pressure, asking the player to remember where the useful passages lead.

cards.heading: A useful misfortune
cards.text: An enemy's attack can give Wario an unexpected ability. A hammer turns him springy enough to jump higher; a sting inflates him into a balloon; another encounter can leave him flat enough to enter a narrow passage. These temporary forms change the available route. A creature that interrupts progress in one place may supply the transformation needed to reach something elsewhere.

cards.heading: Before the treasure goes
cards.text: Boss fights put another clock beside the treasure. The chests behind the opponent disappear as time passes, making a quick victory worth more. Coins spent on short minigames can earn medals for the item shop, whose purchases help damage a boss. Exploring, practising a minigame and fighting efficiently all contribute to how much Wario carries away from the pyramid.
